sections.heading: C — Sharing the road part two: yielding to emergency vehicles, what to do at a police stop, work zones and flaggers, railroad crossing signs and stops, and parking and driving near streetcars and light rail
sections.markdown:
## C — Sharing the road part two: yielding to emergency vehicles, what to do at a police stop, work zones and flaggers, railroad crossing signs and stops, and parking and driving near streetcars and light rail
Knowledge domain: emergency vehicle and police stop duties, work zone speeds, fines and flaggers, railroad crossing warnings and stop rules, what to do when stuck on tracks, and sharing streets with streetcars and light rail; turning and lane rules near streetcars continue in part C2.

FACT_ID: sec07-F01 | anchor: A01
You must yield to emergency vehicles such as fire trucks, police vehicles and ambulances approaching from any direction with a light or siren on. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec07-F02 | anchor: A01
When you see or hear an emergency vehicle warning, move right away as close to the right side of the road as is safe and stop, but never stop inside an intersection. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec07-F03 | anchor: A01
Do not drive or stop in any way that gets in an emergency vehicle's path, and stay stopped until it has passed or an officer tells you to move. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec07-F04 | anchor: A01
Once an emergency vehicle has gone by, you must keep at least 500 feet behind it. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec07-F05 | anchor: A01
A police vehicle trying to stop you will turn on flashing lights or a siren. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec07-F06 | anchor: A01
When police stop you, pull as far to the right as is safe, stop and turn off the engine, and do not stop in an intersection or pull onto a highway's center median. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec07-F07 | anchor: A01
During a police stop, keep your own movements and your passengers' movements to a minimum, keep your hands on the steering wheel, and have passengers keep their hands in plain view. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec07-F08 | anchor: A01
During a police stop, show your driving privilege or registration only when the officer asks, and stay inside the vehicle unless asked to get out. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec07-F09 | anchor: A01
If a police stop happens after dark, turn on the interior light once you have stopped and before the officer reaches you. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec07-F10 | anchor: A01
Do not argue with the officer at a stop, because traffic violations and traffic crimes charged against you are decided in court. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec07-F11 | anchor: A02
Work zones are marked by orange traffic control devices, and workers and construction equipment may be working close to traffic. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec07-F12 | anchor: A02
Traffic fines are doubled in every work zone, and drivers are expected to yield to workers. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec07-F13 | anchor: A02
Signs, cones, flaggers and lane markings guide you through a work zone; orange signs warn of what is ahead and orange cones steer you away from the construction. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec07-F14 | anchor: A02
A temporary speed posted in a work zone applies at all times, even when no workers can be seen. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec07-F15 | anchor: A02
The lower work zone limit holds until a sign ends it, either an End Work Zone Speed Limit sign or a different posted speed limit. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec07-F16 | anchor: A02
On two-lane roads, expect to be stopped in work zones by flaggers or automated devices, and flaggers use signs and hand signals to tell you which way to go, to slow or to stop. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec07-F17 | anchor: A02
An automated flagger device does the same job as a human flagger and has red and yellow lights plus a stop arm. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec07-F18 | anchor: A02
At an automated flagger device, stop while the red light is on and the arm is lowered, and go when the yellow light flashes and the arm is raised. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0067]

FACT_ID: sec07-F19 | anchor: A03
In a freeway work zone you usually keep driving through it, but lanes may be fewer, narrower or newly placed, and you should expect to merge. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec07-F20 | anchor: A03
Freeway work zones can put you very close to cones, workers and equipment, so slow down and pay attention. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec07-F21 | anchor: A03
Do not follow construction vehicles while in a work zone, and expect them to enter the road and slow traffic. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec07-F22 | anchor: A04
When you see railroad crossing signs or signals, look, listen and slow down, because you may need to stop. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec07-F23 | anchor: A04
A railroad advance sign warns that a railroad crossing is ahead. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec07-F24 | anchor: A04
A railroad crossbuck assembly includes a yield or stop sign that you must obey, and where there are several tracks a sign under the crossbuck shows how many. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec07-F25 | anchor: A04
A crossing signal system has flashing red lights and may have a gate with flashing red lights that activate when a train is near. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec07-F26 | anchor: A04
Pavement markings at railroad crossings show a large X with the letters RR. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec07-F27 | anchor: A04
Cross the tracks only when you are sure your vehicle can clear the crossing completely. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec07-F28 | anchor: A04
Never stop on the tracks and never try to beat a train to a crossing. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec07-F29 | anchor: A04
A train you see is closer than it appears, and trains cannot stop quickly. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec07-F30 | anchor: A04
School buses, hazmat vehicles and some school activity vehicles must stop at every railroad crossing, so be ready to stop when following one. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec07-F31 | anchor: A04
One train can hide a second train from your view at a crossing. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec07-F32 | anchor: A05
When you must stop at a railroad crossing, stop at the stop line, or if there is none, at least 15 feet from the nearest rail. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec07-F33 | anchor: A05
Stop before the tracks when the flashing red lights are on, or when a train is clearly visible or so near that crossing would be hazardous. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec07-F34 | anchor: A05
Stop before the tracks when a stop sign is posted, even with no train in sight, and when a flagger signals you to stop. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec07-F35 | anchor: A05
Driving around or under a crossing gate while it is down, rising or lowering is illegal and extremely dangerous. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec07-F36 | anchor: A05
After stopping at a crossing, start across only when you are sure it is safe, and at multiple tracks look both ways for a second train on another track. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec07-F37 | anchor: A05
If a vehicle, person or object is stuck on the tracks, first get out of the vehicle, then move away from the tracks even if no train is in sight. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec07-F38 | anchor: A05
If it is safe, find the Emergency Notification System (ENS) sign on a post near the tracks and use it to tell the railroad about the blockage so it can warn trains. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec07-F39 | anchor: A05
If a train is coming while you are stuck, move away at a 45 degree angle from the tracks toward the direction the train is coming from, so flying debris does not hit you. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec07-F40 | anchor: A06
Streetcars and light rail trains are electric transit vehicles on tracks set in the street; they sometimes share lanes with cars and stop often for passengers, much like buses. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec07-F41 | anchor: A06
Always let streetcars and light rail trains go first, and do not try to pass one unless it is safe. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec07-F42 | anchor: A06
When a streetcar or train stops to let people on or off, stay behind it until it moves again or the people are safely clear. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec07-F43 | anchor: A06
Approaching tracks at an intersection, stay behind any stop line before you cross the tracks. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec07-F44 | anchor: A06
Tracks are never a parking spot: leave your car behind the solid white line that marks off the track area, or where there is no line, close to the curb and as far from the rails as possible. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec07-F45 | anchor: A06
Check for approaching streetcars or trains before opening a door, and make sure your parked vehicle is fully clear of the tracks. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0073]

Misconceptions: you do not pull right in the middle of an intersection for a siren, you clear it first; a work zone speed applies even when no workers are visible; a crossbuck is not a sign to just slow down, it carries a yield or stop sign you obey; a raised or rising gate is still not permission to go around; when stuck, you run toward the train at an angle, not straight away down the tracks.
Mnemonics: siren means right, stop, wait, then stay back; orange means slow and doubled fines; look, listen, slow at every crossbuck; get out, get away, report it at the ENS sign; streetcars go first.
Glossary: work zone means a road area marked by orange traffic control devices; automated flagger means a signal device with red and yellow lights and a stop arm; crossbuck means the X-shaped railroad crossing sign assembly; ENS sign means the Emergency Notification System sign at a crossing; light rail means an electric train running on tracks in the street.
Dynamic facts: work zones are temporary, so their posted speeds and layouts change with the project, and automated flagger and crossing signals change state as traffic and trains move.
